Photograph: Drew Angerer/Getty Images US immigration Far-right media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos deported by ICE from US to UK Ex-Breitbart editor has vocally supported immediate deportations for anyone who can’t prove US residency Edward Helmore Sat 29 Aug 2026 13.08 EDT Last modified on Sat 29 Aug 2026 15.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Far-right British media provocateur Milo Yiannopoulos has been deported from the US after being detained on Thursday by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) in New Orleans in connection with what the agency said was expired authorization to be in the country and a deportation order. Yiannopoulos’s deportation to the UK occurred on Friday, said a statement on Saturday from a spokesperson for the US Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE. A DHS spokesperson on Friday said that Yiannopoulos, 41, had been arrested by ICE on Thursday at the Louis Armstrong New Orleans international airport. The spokesperson said Yiannopoulos “legally entered the country” in May 2019 through New York City but then “chose to overstay his welcome in violation of our nation’s laws”. The spokesperson said that Yiannopoulos was issued a final order of removal by an immigration judge on 22 July “after failing to show up for his immigration hearing”. The spokesperson added: “This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport.” Yiannopoulos – who has previously been a vocal supporter of ICE and immediate deportations for anyone who can’t prove US residency – was believed to have been arrested while heading to a concert by rapper Ye, formerly Kanye West. West performed at New Orleans’s Caesars Superdome on Friday. In 2022, Yiannopoulos worked on West’s short-lived 2024 White House campaign, and his social media account suggests he was working for a company of the rapper. Yiannopoulos, a former editor of the conservative media outlet Breitbart News , previously served as an intern for the former US congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene. He eventually became locked into a feud with fellow far-right commentator Laura Loomer, a Trump administration ally who claimed on Friday that she had reported Yiannopoulos to ICE over his immigration status. At the peak of his influence, Yiannopoulos was offered a speaking slot at the Conservative Political Action Conference, or CPAC, in 2017 after he had been supportive of Donald Trump during his run for his first presidency. He fell out of favor in conservative circles after the publication of a video in which he condoned sexual relations with boys as young as 13. Yiannopoulos claimed that his experiences as a victim of teenage sexual abuse gave him license to comment on the subject. He soon resigned as a senior editor at Breitbart . Yiannopoulos was also banned from Twitter, now called X, in 2016 for directing racist and misogynistic tweets against a Black actor in a Ghostbusters remake. His account was reinstated to the platform in 2022 after it was acquired and renamed by multibillionaire Elon Musk. A little more than a year before his detention by ICE, a social media post from Yiannopoulos called on immigration checkpoints to be set up at California “supermarket entrances, gas stations, strip malls, intersection and government buildings, with on the spot deportation for anyone who can’t prove they are in the US legally”. He had also sarcastically asked whether it was impolite for one “to masturbate” in public rather than in private “if you are going about your business and find yourself observing an ICE raid” amid the mass deportation campaign that Trump has pursued throughout his second presidency. https://www.politico.eu/article/ngo-brus.text: Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babiš’ links to the agro-chemical giant Agrofert represent a conflict of interest and EU subsidies could be withheld as a result, according to an NGO’s account of a letter it received from the European Commission. Ahead of his return to power in December 2025, Babiš placed Agrofert in a trust fund in an effort to preserve its eligibility for EU farm cash. However, that appears not to have convinced Brussels. Transparency International Czechia quotes a letter from DG AGRI Director-General Elisabeth Werner, confirming that “the Commission concluded that Mr Babiš’ situation constitutes a conflict of interest” under EU financial regulations. The trust fund and “measures currently being implemented and notified to the Commission are insufficient” to resolve it, she adds, according to the watchdog NGO, which said it was not allowed to publish the letter. Advertisement Advertisement Babiš has been under renewed scrutiny over Agrofert — a large agro-chemical conglomerate and a major recipient of EU funds — as well as other companies since his return to power last year. Babiš placed the company in a trust fund in a bid to avoid a conflict of interest, but the arrangement has raised questions from both the Commission and the Czech opposition , partly because his children would benefit from it after his death. Babiš has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing. “I don’t own Agrofert, I never will again and I don’t benefit from it in any way. I don’t know what else I’m supposed to do,” he told Czech media last month. “Apparently, even if I shot myself, it still wouldn’t be enough.” Babiš’ office did not immediately reply to POLITICO’s request for comment about the contents of the letter. Werner warned in the letter that Brussels would take all necessary steps to protect EU funds, “including the possible interruption of payment deadlines, suspension of payments or application of financial corrections,” according to TI Czechia. TI Czechia Executive Director David Kotora told POLITICO that he received the letter in September. A follow-up letter from Werner dated Oct. 5 gives the NGO permission to share the contents of the letter without publishing it. The conflict-of-interest dispute echoes Babiš’ first term as prime minister, when a Commission audit found he still controlled Agrofert. That left Czech taxpayers to foot the bill for EU subsidies deemed to be erroneously paid. History could now repeat itself as Brussels last month froze €3.18 million in reimbursements to the Czech state for farm subsidies paid out to Agrofert. That followed its earlier May decision that it would not reimburse any paid-out subsidies until doubts about his involvement in the business could be put to rest. Commission spokesperson Louise Bogey confirmed it had sent a letter to TI Czechia in September, but would not comment on its content. However, she pointed to her remarks at a Sept. 8 midday briefing , during which she said Babiš was in a “potential conflict of interest” and that “the Commission considers the trust fund set up by Mr. Babiš does not sufficiently mitigate this situation.” Czechia’s agricultural paying agency, which earlier decided that the conglomerate is eligible for EU subsidies despite the Commission’s warning, said Tuesday it had sent clarifications to the Commission this week. Agrofert spokesperson Pavel Heřmanský said neither Agrofert nor any of its subsidiaries were involved in the communication between the Commission and Czech authorities. “The cited letter from DG AGRI expresses the opinion of one of the European Commission’s departments. It does not constitute an official position of the European Commission,” said Heřmanský in a statement, adding that “only the Court of Justice of the European Union can provide a binding interpretation of European Union law.” He added: “We remain convinced that we have received and continue to receive subsidies in compliance with both Czech and European law.”
